groups.instructionTh: อ่านบทความต่อไปนี้ แล้วตอบคำถามโดยเลือกคำตอบที่ถูกต้องที่สุด
groups.title: Life Without Sunlight
groups.text:
Until the late 1970s, most biologists assumed that the deep ocean floor was something close to a desert. Far below the reach of sunlight, where temperatures hover just above freezing and the pressure is hundreds of times greater than at the surface, life was thought to exist only in scattered form, surviving on the thin "marine snow" of dead plankton drifting down from above. The discovery of hydrothermal vents overturned that picture almost overnight.

Hydrothermal vents form where the plates of the Earth's crust are slowly pulling apart. Seawater seeps down through cracks in the young rock, is heated by magma lying close beneath, and rises again, often at temperatures above 350°C. Because of the immense pressure at these depths, the water does not boil. Instead, it dissolves metals and sulphur compounds from the surrounding rock. When this superheated fluid meets the near-freezing seawater, the dissolved minerals precipitate out, building chimney-like structures that can grow several metres in a matter of months. The darkest of these, nicknamed "black smokers," release clouds of fine metal particles that look strikingly like smoke.

What astonished the first observers, however, was not the geology but the crowds of animals clustered around the chimneys: pale crabs, dense beds of mussels, and tube worms taller than a person, topped with bright red plumes. Such abundance seemed impossible in total darkness. The explanation lies in a process called chemosynthesis. Certain bacteria are able to extract energy from chemicals in the vent fluid, particularly hydrogen sulphide, and use it to turn carbon dioxide into organic matter, much as plants use the energy of sunlight. These microbes form the base of the vent food web. Some live freely as mats on the rocks; others live inside the bodies of animals. The giant tube worms, for example, have no mouth or gut as adults. They depend entirely on billions of bacteria housed in a specialised organ. The worms deliver the chemicals these microbes need through their blood, and in exchange the microbes give them a share of the food they produce.

Vent communities are also remarkably temporary. A single vent may remain active for only a few decades before shifting geological activity cuts off its supply of hot fluid, and the animals that rely on it then die off. How vent species manage to colonise new sites, which may lie hundreds of kilometres apart, remains one of the field's open questions. One hypothesis, supported by a recent survey led by marine ecologist Dr. Helena Varga of the Northbridge Ocean Institute, is that larvae drift on deep currents for months, surviving in a low-energy state until they encounter the chemical signature of an active vent.

Interest in vents now extends well beyond biology. Some researchers argue that environments like these, rich in chemical energy and sheltered from harsh conditions at the surface, may resemble the settings in which life on Earth first emerged. At the same time, the metal deposits around vents have drawn the attention of mining companies, raising concerns that ecosystems scientists have barely begun to study could be damaged before they are properly understood.

groups.title: Paper on the Move
groups.text:
Of all the goods that travelled along the network of trade routes now known as the Silk Road, few changed the world as profoundly as paper. Silk, spices and porcelain were luxuries enjoyed by a wealthy few. Paper, by contrast, eventually transformed the way ordinary societies kept records, educated their children and spread ideas.

Paper was developed in China, where early versions made from hemp and other plant fibres were in use more than two thousand years ago. Compared with the materials it gradually replaced, such as bamboo strips, which were heavy, and silk, which was costly, it was light, cheap and easy to produce in large quantities. For several centuries, however, the knowledge of how to make it stayed largely within East Asia. Merchants carried finished sheets westward, but the techniques themselves were not widely shared.

A traditional account holds that the craft reached Central Asia in the eighth century, when papermakers taken prisoner during a conflict were brought to the city of Samarkand and put to work there. Historians today treat this story with some caution. As the historian Idris Halvorsen has observed, the tale is tidy in a way that real history rarely is; technologies seldom spread through a single dramatic event. Fragments recovered from old caravan towns suggest that paper was already being used, and perhaps produced, in the region before that date. What is clear is that within a few generations Samarkand, and then Baghdad, had become major centres of paper manufacture.

The craft did not simply pass from one place to the next unchanged. Papermakers in Central Asia and the Middle East, who lacked the mulberry bark and bamboo used in China, turned instead to linen rags, which were plentiful in growing cities. They also developed methods of coating the sheets with starch so that ink would not soak in, producing a smooth surface well suited to the flowing scripts used in government and scholarship. These adaptations were not minor details: they made paper practical in a new region with different resources and different writing traditions.

The consequences were far-reaching. Government offices that had relied on parchment, made from animal skin, could now keep much larger archives at a fraction of the cost. Book markets flourished, and libraries grew to sizes that would have been unthinkable a few centuries earlier. Mathematicians and astronomers filled notebooks with calculations and observations that could be copied and circulated. From there, paper moved on through North Africa and into Europe, where water-powered mills were operating by the twelfth and thirteenth centuries.

It is tempting to describe this history as a straight line of progress, but doing so hides the role of the many anonymous craftspeople who experimented, failed and adjusted along the way. The story of paper is less about a single invention than about thousands of small decisions made by people who never imagined how much their work would matter.

groups.title: Understanding Inflation
groups.text:
Few economic terms appear in the news as often as inflation, yet it is frequently misunderstood. In simple terms, inflation is a sustained rise in the general level of prices across an economy. The key words are "sustained" and "general." A sudden jump in the price of mangoes after a poor harvest is not, by itself, inflation; nor is a one-off increase in the cost of a single service. Inflation describes a situation in which the prices of a wide range of goods and services rise steadily over time, so that each unit of money buys less than it did before.

Economists usually measure inflation with a price index. Statisticians select a "basket" of goods and services that a typical household buys, such as food, rent, transport, electricity and school fees, and track how much that basket costs from month to month. If the basket cost 10,000 baht last year and 10,300 baht this year, the annual inflation rate is 3 percent. The method is not perfect. Households in the countryside and in large cities spend their money differently, and the basket must be updated as new products appear and old ones disappear. Even so, the index offers a useful snapshot of how prices are moving.

Why do prices rise in the first place? Economists generally point to two broad causes. The first, known as demand-pull inflation, occurs when total spending in an economy grows faster than the economy's ability to produce goods and services. Too much money, in effect, is chasing too few goods, and sellers respond by raising prices. The second, cost-push inflation, begins on the supply side. When the costs of production increase, because of higher fuel prices or rising wages, for instance, firms pass at least part of those costs on to their customers. In practice, the two often occur together and can be difficult to separate.

Moderate inflation is not necessarily harmful. Many central banks deliberately aim for a low, stable rate, often around two percent. A little inflation gives the economy some flexibility and is considered less damaging than its opposite, deflation, in which falling prices can encourage consumers to postpone purchases and so slow down economic activity. What causes real difficulty is high or unpredictable inflation. When prices rise quickly, people on fixed incomes, such as retirees living on pensions, find that their money covers less and less. Savings kept in cash lose value. Businesses, uncertain about future costs, may delay investment.

Consider a café owner, whom we will call Ploy. If her costs for milk, coffee beans and electricity rise by 8 percent in a year, she faces an uncomfortable choice. She can raise her prices and risk losing customers, or keep them unchanged and accept lower profits. Multiply that dilemma across millions of businesses and households, and it becomes clear why governments watch inflation figures so closely.

The main tool central banks use to control inflation is the interest rate. Raising rates makes borrowing more expensive and saving more attractive, which tends to reduce spending and ease pressure on prices. The difficulty lies in timing: changes in interest rates can take many months to have their full effect, so policymakers must act on forecasts rather than certainties.

groups.title: What the Sleeping Brain Does
groups.text:
For much of history, sleep was regarded as a period when the brain simply switched off. Research over the past several decades has painted a very different picture. Far from being idle, the sleeping brain appears to be busy with an important task: sorting, strengthening and reorganising the memories formed during the day.

Psychologists distinguish between encoding, the process of taking in new information, and consolidation, the slower process by which a fragile new memory becomes stable and long-lasting. Consolidation can take place while we are awake, but a growing body of evidence suggests that sleep provides especially favourable conditions for it. One influential idea holds that during certain stages of sleep the brain "replays" patterns of activity that occurred during learning. Recordings in laboratory animals have shown that cells which were active while an animal explored a maze fire again, in the same order, while it sleeps afterward, often at a much faster speed.

Not all sleep is the same. Over a night, the brain cycles through several stages, including deep, slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, the stage most associated with vivid dreaming. Researchers have proposed that these stages play different roles. Slow-wave sleep has been linked mainly to memory for facts and events, while REM sleep may be more involved in emotional memories and in skills. These divisions, however, are far from settled, and many scientists now believe that the stages work together rather than separately.

A study carried out at the Larchmont Institute of Cognitive Science illustrates the kind of evidence researchers rely on. Sixty university students learned a list of word pairs in the evening. Half then slept normally, while the other half stayed awake through the night under supervision. Both groups were then allowed a full night of recovery sleep before being tested, so that tiredness on the day of the test could not account for any difference between them. Those who had slept immediately after learning recalled noticeably more pairs. Interestingly, the advantage was greatest for the pairs the students had found most difficult, suggesting that sleep may give priority to information that was only weakly learned.

Findings like these have sometimes been exaggerated in popular articles, with claims that people can pick up a new language by listening to recordings while they sleep. The evidence for such claims is weak. Most researchers stress that sleep appears to strengthen what has already been learned rather than allowing entirely new material to be absorbed from scratch. Studies in this area are also typically small, and results obtained in carefully controlled laboratories do not always hold in everyday life.

What does seem clear is that learning and sleep are more closely connected than was once believed. For students who regularly trade sleep for extra hours of late-night study, the research raises an uncomfortable question: whether the hours gained are worth the consolidation that may be lost.

groups.title: Building for Weight and Weather
groups.text:
Visitors to historic temples and mosques often focus on their decoration: gilded panels, carved stucco, and glazed tiles in deep blues and greens. Yet some of the most impressive achievements of these buildings are hidden in plain sight, in the way they solve practical problems of structure and climate using materials and techniques that existed long before modern engineering.

Consider the dome. Placing a round dome on top of a square room is far more difficult than it appears, because the circular base of the dome does not match the square walls beneath it. Builders in West and Central Asia developed two main solutions. The squinch is an arch built diagonally across each upper corner of the square, turning it into an octagon that is much closer to a circle. The pendentive, a curved triangular section of masonry, creates a smoother transition, gathering the weight of the dome and channelling it down to four corner supports. Both techniques allowed builders to roof large interior spaces without forests of columns, and both later became decorative features in their own right, often covered with intricate honeycomb-like carving.

In mainland Southeast Asia, by contrast, the main challenge was not spanning space but shedding water. Where monsoon rains can fall heavily for months, roofs had to move huge volumes of water away from walls of brick and lime plaster, which could weaken if constantly soaked. The steep, layered roofs familiar from many historic temples in Thailand, Laos and Myanmar respond to this problem. Overlapping tiers allow a roof to stay steep enough to drain quickly while keeping its overall height manageable, and deep overhanging eaves protect the walls below. The tiers also reduce the visual bulk of the roof, giving even large halls a sense of lightness.

Climate shaped interiors as well. In hot, dry cities, many mosques were arranged around open courtyards, sometimes with a central pool. Shaded arcades around the courtyard offered cool places to walk, while water and stone surfaces helped to moderate temperatures. Thick walls absorbed heat during the day and released it slowly at night. In humid tropical settings, builders generally favoured the opposite strategy: rather than storing coolness, they encouraged air to move. High ceilings, tall doors and rows of windows on opposite walls allowed breezes to pass through, carrying away heat and moisture.

The architectural historian Dr. Malin Charoenwet argues that these buildings should be read as "records of experiment." Many of them show signs of repairs and later modifications, suggesting that builders learned from failures such as cracked walls, collapsed vaults and leaking roofs, and adjusted their methods over generations. Restoration specialists today face a delicate task. Replacing traditional lime plaster with modern cement, for example, may seem like an improvement, but because cement traps moisture rather than allowing it to evaporate, it has in some cases accelerated the very decay it was meant to prevent.

groups.title: Science by the Crowd
groups.text:
When astronomers at the Westmere Observatory found themselves with more than a million images of distant galaxies and no practical way to classify them all, they tried an unusual solution: they asked the public for help. Within weeks of launching a simple website, tens of thousands of volunteers had signed up to sort galaxies by shape. The project completed in a few months a task the researchers had estimated would take a single specialist several decades.

Projects like this are known as citizen science or crowd-sourced science: research in which members of the public, most with no formal scientific training, help to collect or analyse data. The idea is not entirely new. Amateur naturalists have recorded bird sightings and weather observations for centuries, and some of those records remain valuable today. What has changed is scale. Smartphones, inexpensive sensors and the internet now allow projects to recruit participants from around the world and to process their contributions almost instantly.

The range of projects is wide. Volunteers photograph insects in their gardens, count frogs calling in roadside ponds, transcribe handwritten ship logs from the nineteenth century, and play online puzzle games whose solutions help scientists predict the shapes of complex molecules. In the Mekong Rain Watch project, more than 4,000 households in three countries measured daily rainfall with simple plastic gauges, filling the gaps between official weather stations that can be more than fifty kilometres apart.

Not everyone was convinced at first. Critics worried that data gathered by untrained volunteers would be too unreliable to be useful. These concerns were not unreasonable, and project designers have responded in several ways. Many tasks are shown to several volunteers, so that one person's mistakes are outweighed by the agreement of the majority. Some projects include items whose correct classification is already known, which allows organisers to check each participant's accuracy. Still others ask volunteers to say how confident they are in each answer, so that uncertain cases can be passed on to experts. Studies comparing volunteer and expert results have often found the two to be remarkably close, particularly for tasks that are clearly defined.

The benefits are not only scientific. Participants frequently report that they understand the research process better and feel a stronger connection to nature or to the subject they are helping to study. Volunteers also sometimes notice what professionals miss. In the frog-counting project, for instance, a retired engineer observed that one species had stopped calling at several ponds near a newly built highway, an observation that led to a formal study of the effects of road noise.

Crowd-sourced science also raises difficult questions. Volunteers may contribute hundreds of hours of work, yet they are rarely named in the papers that result. Some researchers argue that participants deserve clearer recognition and more say in how projects are designed, rather than being treated simply as a free source of labour. As citizen science continues to grow, finding a fair balance between the interests of professional scientists and those of the public is likely to become one of its central challenges.
